title: Four-dimensional X-ray nano-holotomography reveals multiscale chemomechanics in composite graphite–silicon battery electrodes
content:
Nature Nanotechnology, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41565-026-02327-6

Particle-resolved 4D nano-tomography identifies fast ionic transport pathways as key regulators of electrochemical activity and reversibility in graphite–silicon battery electrodes.
summary: Particle-resolved time-lapse nano-holotomography on composite graphite–silicon electrodes links local ionic transport pathways to electrochemical activity and reversibility. This gives multiscale chemomechanical heterogeneity (particle-to-particle, network-level) in a commercially relevant composite. Only the abstract teaser was available, so quantitative details are unverified.

title: Tracking local chemomechanics in graphite–silicon composite electrodes
content:
Nature Nanotechnology, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41565-026-02328-5

Operando 4D imaging reveals how local ionic pathways govern activity in graphite–silicon battery electrodes.
summary: Operando 4D imaging of graphite–silicon composite electrodes links local ionic pathways to particle-level activity and chemomechanics. This addresses spatial heterogeneity in a commercially relevant blend. The abstract is brief, so the quantitative findings and exact modality can't be checked.

title: Stage‐Specific Pressure Programming Decouples Low‐Pressure Sulfur Reduction From High‐Pressure Interfacial Reconstruction in All‐Solid‐State Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
content:
Stage‐specific pressure programming decouples low‐pressure sulfur reduction from high‐pressure interfacial reconstruction in all‐solid‐state lithium–sulfur batteries. Combining 1 MPa discharge with 180 MPa charge enables 98.8% capacity retention over 100 cycles with 50 wt% sulfur cathodes. This pressure dichotomy offers a route to easing the trade‐off between energy density, cycle life, and stack pressure.








ABSTRACT
The commercialization of all‐solid‐state Li–S batteries (ASSLSBs) remains constrained by the “impossible trinity” between high energy density, long cycle life, and low stack pressure. Here we show that stack pressure is not merely a static mechanical boundary, but a stage‐specific regulator of sulfur conversion and interfacial reconstruction. Using a static pressure‐resistance‐overpotential (P‐R‐η) operational threshold algorithm, low‐stack‐pressure operation is predicted feasible for 50 wt% S cathodes. Further operando electrochemical measurements and multiscale chemical and structural characterizations reveal that 1 MPa discharge promotes Li2S2‐rich interfacial intermediates. However, constant low‐pressure cycling induces progressive pore filling that prolongs charge transport pathways, leading to inactive LiXS accumulation and triphase interfacial contact losses. State‐resolved very‐small‐angle neutron scattering (VSANS) further uncovers a ∼5 nm structural feature that persists after low‐stack‐pressure discharge, which specifically diminishes upon high‐pressure charging. Guided by this mechanism, we implement a pressure‐programmed protocol combining 1 MPa discharge with 180 MPa charge. The resulting cell retains 98.8% of capacity after 100 cycles at 30 °C. This work establishes a dynamic pressure modulation strategy towards alleviating the “impossible trinity” by decoupling the asymmetric pressure‐electrochemical behaviors.
journal: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
summary: Shows that stack pressure acts stage-specifically in all-solid-state Li–S cells. Low-pressure cycling fills pores and accumulates inactive LiXS. State-resolved VSANS finds a ~5 nm feature that persists after 1 MPa discharge and disappears on high-pressure charge. This led to a 1 MPa discharge / 180 MPa charge protocol with 98.8% retention over 100 cycles. Mechanistic evidence is partly indirect.

title:
Transition-Metal-Mediated
Discharge Intermediates
Set Anionic-Redox Potentials and Voltage Hysteresis in Li-Rich Cathodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Voltage hysteresis arising from anionic redox reactions remains a central bottleneck for lithium-rich cathodes. While ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) has been invoked to describe the charging pathway, its proposed reverse counterpart, metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT), remains experimentally unresolved during discharge. Here, using cation-disordered rock-salt Li2Ni0.33Ta0.66O3 (LNTO) as a model system, we combine electrochemical relaxation analysis with synchrotron-based spectroscopy to identify, for the first time, a metastable reduction intermediate characterized by Ni(2-δ)+/(O–O)n− during discharge, thereby providing direct experimental validation for the MLCT framework. The discovery of this metastable intermediate demonstrates that discharge proceeds through a two-step electrochemical–chemical pathway, wherein the spontaneous relaxation evolution of the metastable intermediate drives free-energy dissipation and voltage hysteresis. Guided by this picture, Ru substitution was introduced to modulate the cation–anion electronic structure, enabling Ru 4d–O 2p hybridization to generate persistent low-energy hole states that lower the energy of the metastable discharge intermediate and shift O–O dimer reduction to higher potentials. We further show that the discharge intermediate serves as the energetic link through which transition-metal electronic structure governs the effective anionic-redox potential. This work provides a discharge-side thermodynamic framework for understanding and mitigating voltage hysteresis in Li-rich anionic-redox cathodes.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society
summary: Claims first experimental evidence of a metastable Ni(2-δ)+/(O–O)n− discharge intermediate (MLCT) in a DRX Li2Ni0.33Ta0.66O3, showing relaxation of this intermediate drives voltage hysteresis. Ru substitution then shifts O–O reduction potential upward. The mechanism is interesting, but the evidence is bulk spectroscopy, not spatially resolved.

title: Contouring mitigates voiding at the lithium/ceramic electrolyte interface on discharging solid-state batteries
content:
Nature Energy, Published online: 23 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41560-026-02172-w

Discharge-induced voids are a major barrier to practical lithium metal solid-state batteries. Here the authors show that an egg-box-contoured lithium–electrolyte interface increases the voiding threshold by an order of magnitude and enables realistic electric vehicle discharge profiles without polarization.
summary: A geometric "egg-box" contoured Li/ceramic interface raises the critical discharge current density for void formation by about 10x. It also supports EV-like discharge profiles without polarization. This addresses a key failure mode in Li-metal solid-state batteries. The abstract doesn't say whether the mechanism was confirmed by direct imaging or by modelling.
technique: patterned Li/ceramic electrolyte interface; electrochemical stripping tests

content:

summary: The abstract is missing, so this judgement rests on the title and the author group. It appears to use operando fiber-optic sensing to track lithium status in commercial-format pouch cells. That would be a transferable operando method from the Tarascon group. It is probably not spatially resolved imaging, and the actual findings can't be assessed.
technique: operando fiber-optic sensing (optical fiber sensors in pouch cells)
